Reb Zalman Chayim stopped to speak to a few more people before ultimately ending up at the beis midrash: a short, portly spice seller; a red-faced teenager with an oversized basket of rolls; a one-eyed beggar shaking a cup that contained but a solitary coin. With each one, Reb Zalman Chayim knew just what to say. For some, it was the promise of

an aliya. For others, it was a few heartfelt words about the value of tefilla. And for yet others, all they needed was Reb Zalman Chayim’s smile to draw them in.

Baruch had already davened shacharis, but he was curious. What was davening like in Reb Zalman Chayim’s minyan?

any other that Baruch had seen. Simple laborers davened alongside men who looked like solid talmidei chachamim. Some of the villagers mispronounced words or said “amen” at the wrong time. No one laughed or corrected them, unlike in the other shuls Baruch had visited.

After krias haTorah was over, Reb Zalman Chayim took out a wooden tzedaka box. In most shuls, this would be the time when the shamash would collect a few pennies for his salary. A few people here and there

would throw a coin his way, and that would be that. But this shul was different.

to the market. Baruch found an empty room, where he settled down with a Gemara. At first, the building was completely silent; after about five

minutes, though, Baruch heard faint sounds coming from the main room. Another minyan was starting. And so it continued for the rest of the morning: minyan after minyan at five-minute intervals, a short break, followed by a shiur around midday; and then, again, minyanim and shiurim until well into the night.

For the majority of his day, Baruch learned alone in the side room. But for a few minutes here and there, before and after davening or on his way out to find a job to replenish his stash

of bread, he’d take some time to watch Reb Zalman Chayim’s work. Baruch never saw the shamash so much as sit down alone or take a rest. From morning to night, Reb Zalman Chayim was busy helping his fellow Yidden. He went from making speeches in the marketplace to running the minyanim; from giving a Chumash and Rashi shiur to distributing the money from the gemach; and somehow, he found time to sit and encourage people in between. On Wednesdays, market days in Yanovitch, Reb Zalman Chayim was especially

busy. First of all, a lot of people needed loans for business. There were also lots more people to speak to, since Jews from the surrounding villages would come into Yanovitch to sell their wares.

them about their families and their parnassa, being sure to inquire if they perhaps needed a loan or some business advice. Then, he’d gently suggest ways

for how they could improve their own Yiddishkeit, and that of their village. Perhaps they could study some Torah every day; perhaps they could band together with nearby Jews and build a shul in their village; perhaps they could hire a melamed to teach their sons Torah. In this way, Reb Zalman Chayim single- handedly transformed many of the outlying hamlets and villages around Yanovitch.

One of the villagers who was deeply affected by Reb Zalman Chayim’s work was a Jew named Mordechai the Miller. Mordechai came to see Reb Zalman Chayim every single Wednesday without fail. With the shamash’s loving encouragement, Mordechai— a rather wealthy man—paid for a shul to be built where he lived. Mordechai’s children were already grown, so he had no need for a melamed, but he showed his newfound value for Torah study by marrying off his two daughters to talmidei chachamim. This, in turn, had another positive effect on Mordechai’s village: The older son-in-law, Avraham Shlomo, started teaching classes in the shul, uplifting the entire community. The villagers— all unlearned, but truly sincere—loved the classes. They were disappointed when Avraham Shlomo accepted a job as a rav in the nearby town, and they immediately began looking for a replacement.
